label: UGC NET June 2026 Paper 2 — Stochastic Processes questions not in the 1–50 set (booklet numbers not known; identified by official question ID)

items.stem: The arrival of customers in a bank follows a Poisson process with rate 2 customers per minute. The probability that the time interval between two successive arrivals is more than 6 minutes, given that it is more than 4 minutes, is
items.explanation: Idea: in a Poisson process the times between arrivals are exponential, and the exponential is memoryless. Having already waited 4 minutes tells you nothing, so only the extra 2 minutes matter. Working: Inter-arrival T ~ Exp(rate 2). Memoryless: P(T > 6 | T > 4) = P(T > 2) = e^(−2·2) = e^(−4). Official answer: B (e^(−4)).

items.stem: Consider a three-state Markov chain with transition probability matrix P = [[0, 1, 0], [0.5, 0, 0.5], [0, 1, 0]], so that P² = [[0.5, 0, 0.5], [0, 1, 0], [0.5, 0, 0.5]] and P³ = P. Then the Markov chain is
items.explanation: Idea: a chain is irreducible if every state can reach every other; the period is the gcd of the step counts at which a return is possible. P² and P³ = P show that returns happen only at even steps. Working: 1↔2↔3 all communicate (irreducible); returns to any state only at even steps (pᵢᵢ⁽ⁿ⁾ > 0 only for even n), period 2. Official answer: B (Irreducible and periodic).

items.stem: Suppose, for a Markov chain, C₁ is the communicating class of state i and C₂ is the communicating class of state j. State k communicates with both i and j. Then
options: k belongs to neither C₁ nor C₂
k has a different period than that of i and j
items.explanation: Idea: 'communicates with' is an equivalence relation, so communicating classes either coincide or do not overlap at all. A state k linking i and j forces i and j into the same class. Working: Communication is an equivalence relation: i↔k and k↔j give i↔j, so C₁ = C₂ (and k is in it, with the same period). Official answer: B (C₁ = C₂).

items.stem: A gambler is playing in a casino with an initial capital of Rs. 100. If the gambler wins, he receives Rs. 1 and if he loses, he pays Rs. 1. The probability that the gambler wins is 3/4. The probability of ultimate ruin of the gambler is
items.explanation: Idea: in gambler's ruin against an opponent with unlimited money, ruin is certain only if the game is fair or unfavourable. Here the gambler is favoured (p = 3/4), so the ruin probability is less than 1 and shrinks geometrically with the starting capital. Working: Against an infinitely rich adversary with p = 3/4 > q = 1/4, P(ruin from capital a) = (q/p)^a = (1/3)^100. Official answer: D ((1/3)^100).

items.stem: Let N₁(t) and N₂(t) be two independent Poisson processes with parameters λ and 2λ respectively. Then P(N₁(t) = 1 | N₁(t) + N₂(t) = 4) is
items.explanation: Idea: given that two independent Poisson counts add to n, each event belongs to the first process with probability λ₁/(λ₁ + λ₂) independently. So the conditional count is binomial. Working: Given the total is 4, N₁(t) ~ Binomial(4, λ/(λ + 2λ) = 1/3): P = 4·(1/3)·(2/3)³ = 32/81 = 2⁵/3⁴. Official answer: B (2⁵/3⁴).

items.stem: Let us consider a three-state Markov chain with the transition probability matrix P = [[q, p, 0], [q, 0, p], [0, q, p]], where 0 < p < 1, q + p = 1. The three-step transition probability p₁₂⁽³⁾ is
items.explanation: Idea: an n-step transition probability is an entry of Pⁿ. Compute the first row of P², then multiply by the second column of P. Working: Row 1 of P² is (q, pq, p²). p₁₂⁽³⁾ = q·p + pq·0 + p²·q = pq + p²q = pq(1 + p). Official answer: B (pq(1 + p)).

items.stem: Let us consider a three-state Markov chain with the transition probability matrix P = [[q, p, 0], [q, 0, p], [0, q, p]], where 0 < p < 1, q + p = 1. The stationary probability distribution of the Markov chain is
items.explanation: Idea: the stationary distribution solves πP = π with the entries of π adding to 1. Write the balance equations and solve them in terms of p and q. Working: πP = π gives pπ₁ = qπ₂ and pπ₂ = qπ₃, so π ∝ (1, p/q, (p/q)²). This equals (1/3, 1/3, 1/3) only when p = q = 1/2 (then P is doubly stochastic). Source note: For general p the stationary distribution is proportional to (1, p/q, (p/q)²), which is not among the options. The official key (1/3, 1/3, 1/3) is correct only when p = q = 1/2; the column sums of P are 2q, 1, 2p, so P is doubly stochastic only then. Official answer: D ((1/3, 1/3, 1/3)).

items.stem: Let us consider a three-state Markov chain with the transition probability matrix P = [[q, p, 0], [q, 0, p], [0, q, p]], where 0 < p < 1, q + p = 1. The first passage probability f₁₂⁽⁵⁾ is equal to
items.explanation: Idea: a first passage to state 2 at exactly step 5 means not being in state 2 at steps 1–4. From state 1, avoiding 2 means staying at 1. Working: The only way to reach 2 for the first time at step 5 is to stay at 1 for four steps (q⁴) and then move to 2 (p): f₁₂⁽⁵⁾ = q⁴p. Official answer: A (q⁴p).

items.stem: Let us consider a three-state Markov chain with the transition probability matrix P = [[q, p, 0], [q, 0, p], [0, q, p]], where 0 < p < 1, q + p = 1. The first return probability to state 1 in three steps, f₁₁⁽³⁾, is
items.explanation: Idea: list every three-step path that starts at 1 and first comes back to 1 at step 3, and check which transitions it needs. If any needed transition has probability 0, the path is impossible. Working: A first return in three steps needs 1 → 2 → x → 1 with x ≠ 1. p₂₂ = 0 and p₃₁ = 0, so no such path exists and f₁₁⁽³⁾ = 0. Official answer: C (0).

items.stem: Let us consider a three-state Markov chain with the transition probability matrix P = [[q, p, 0], [q, 0, p], [0, q, p]], where 0 < p < 1, q + p = 1. The expected number of steps required for a transition from state 1 to state 2 (μ₁₂) is
items.explanation: Idea: from state 1 the only moves are 'stay' or 'go to 2'. Waiting for the first move to 2 is a run of independent trials with success probability p, so the waiting time is geometric. Working: From state 1 the chain either stays (probability q) or moves to 2 (probability p), so the number of steps to reach 2 is geometric with success probability p and mean 1/p. Official answer: D (p⁻¹).
